pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: An expert is a person who has never been wrong in public.*

Rue did not sit. She remained standing under the chestnut tree, her boots muddy from the run, and talked. It came out sideways, all at once, in one great, breathless tangle of words about the moss, the spectacles, the toothache, and the net.

Perrin Fen listened without blinking, holding his notebook against his chest like a shield while his ink-stained fingers stayed planted on the cover. When Rue ran out of steam and gasped for air, he looked at her with a calm, steady gaze that made her feel like a very loud bird.

"I knew it," he said.

Rue blinked. "You did?"

"I mean, I didn't know it," Perrin corrected, his voice flat and dry. "I knew there was something under there that was good. It is a fact."

He opened his notebook to a fresh page and clicked his pencil. "What does the Mayor need to change his mind?" he asked. "That is the useful question."
pages.image: A small freckled girl with red hair in puffs stands anxiously before a thin quiet boy in an oversized wool hat under a large chestnut tree, the boy holding a notebook while looking at her with calm, steady eyes.

pages.text:
Plan A was a letter. It was the most sensible thing Rue had ever done, which is saying something, because her usual plan was to run and hide.

Perrin’s handwriting was excellent. Small, neat, and slanted slightly to the left, the words lined up like a row of polite sheep. He wrote that the troll was a gentle librarian who maintained the bridge. He wrote that he was not hungry, only thirsty for stories. He wrote that he was tired.

They walked to the town hall. The Mayor was in his office, polishing his chain of office. He held the letter up to the light, reading the first two sentences in a high, squeaky voice that sounded like a duck being stepped on.

"A gentle librarian," he wheezed, and then he laughed.

The committee members behind him giggled. The Mayor rolled the paper into a tight cylinder and flicked it into the air. It landed on the floor with a soft thud.

"Denied," he said, and went back to polishing.
pages.image: A round pompous man in a top hat holds a rolled paper and laughs loudly at a desk, while a small girl and a boy in a wool hat stand by the door looking dismayed.

pages.text:
Plan B was to talk to Skye.

Rue found her in the yard, braiding her hair with a red ribbon. Skye was tall and golden, and she turned when she heard Rue’s voice.

"Skye, it’s not a monster. It’s Hobb. He reads. He mends the stones."

Skye stopped braiding. Her face turned a bright, angry pink, the color of a beetroot that has been squeezed too hard.

"Rue, you mean well," she said, her voice tight. "But everyone knows what is under that bridge. You can’t just decide it’s nice. That’s not how it works."

Rue opened her mouth to argue. She wanted to say that nice is a choice. She wanted to say that knowing is better than guessing. But the words stuck in her throat, because she realized Skye was right. She had never once asked the town to look. She had only ever asked them to stop.
pages.image: A tall girl with a long fair braid frowns at a small freckled girl in a mustard raincoat in a schoolyard, her expression serious and annoyed as she holds a red ribbon.

pages.text:
Plan C was hiding in the notebook.

Perrin flipped past the letter to a page crowded with tiny, precise drawings. They showed the old bridge, but not the whole thing, only the middle arch seen from below.

"I have been measuring," Perrin said, tapping a line of numbers. "Every year, the middle sags half a finger-width more. The stone is cracking. By next winter, it will fall. That is what the mathematics say."

"But it hasn’t fallen," Rue said.

"No," Perrin agreed. "It hasn’t. And that is impossible, unless someone is fixing it."

He looked up, his eyes wide and bright. "I can prove it. I can show them the numbers. Numbers do not lie, and numbers do not laugh."

Rue looked at the drawing. It looked like a skeleton of stone, thin and fragile. "Right then," she whispered.
pages.image: A close-up of a notebook page showing a detailed drawing of a stone arch bridge with measurement lines, held by a boy with ink-stained fingers, with a small girl looking over his shoulder.

pages.text:
When they reached the bridge, the air under the arch was cold and smelled of damp paper.

Hobb was there. He was sitting on a bucket, his mossy shoulders hunched high. His books were unpacked, then packed, then unpacked again on the floor around him. He looked like a storm that had forgotten how to rain.

When he saw Rue, his ears perked up. When he saw the stranger beside her, he froze. The humming of the kettle behind him stopped. The silence was so sudden it felt like a punch.

Perrin stepped forward. He held out his notebook, open to the drawing of the arch. He did not smile. He did not look away.

"You’re better than I imagined," Perrin said.

Hobb looked at the drawing. He looked at Rue. He looked at the bucket beneath his feet.

And then, very suddenly, he sat down on it. The wood groaned under his weight.
pages.image: A large mossy troll with round spectacles sits heavily on a wooden bucket under a stone arch, looking at a small notebook held by a boy in a wool hat, while a small girl watches with worry.
